claims.text: A combined high-throughput DSC, in-situ X-ray scattering, and CALPHAD approach can determine HEA melting and liquid-phase properties accurately.
The approach will achieve roughly 5–10% accuracy for melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
The proposed accuracy applies to HEAs containing 4–8 principal components.
The target materials are equiatomic or near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloys in as-cast or homogenized states.
CALPHAD can calculate multicomponent phase equilibria by minimizing Gibbs energy supplied by thermodynamic databases.
High-throughput CALPHAD calculations can efficiently explore large HEA composition spaces.
DSC and in-situ synchrotron X-ray scattering can be applied systematically over approximately 800–2000 K and across the full composition ranges of candidate HEAs.
Controlled inert or vacuum environments and calibrated DSC protocols enable reliable tracking of melting behavior.
Real-time diffraction can directly track phase boundaries and lattice parameters near and through melting.
Diffraction-derived phase boundaries and lattice parameters can mediate between DSC thermal signals and CALPHAD phase-equilibrium predictions.
Synchronizing DSC data, real-time phase characterization, and CALPHAD Gibbs-energy evaluations captures the enthalpic and entropic response at melting.
X-ray scattering measurements provide the volumetric response or volume change at melting.
The integrated measurements yield robust liquid-phase thermodynamic property data.
The approach will rapidly map composition–property correlations for HEA liquid thermodynamics and melting behavior.
Conventional single-alloy DSC or separate modeling requires extensive alloy-by-alloy trial and error.
Coupling high-throughput screening with validated CALPHAD modeling offers greater speed across broad composition spaces.
The approach is primarily applicable where thermodynamic databases are well calibrated and phases approach equilibrium during DSC.
Metastability, rapid heating, or transient phase transformations can obscure DSC or X-ray measurements and cause deviations.
Accuracy depends on DSC calibration, sample homogeneity, database accuracy, and unaccounted transient transformations.
Systematic differences greater than 10% in melting temperature, enthalpy of fusion, or entropy of fusion relative to independent reference methods would reject the claimed accuracy.
